description:
Peak by Anders Ericsson and Robert Pool, summarized and explained: why an ordinary college student went from 8 to 82 digits, why 10,000 hours guarantees nothing, and why comfort is where improvement stops.

Experts are not people born with a gift, and they are not people who simply logged more hours. In this deep-dive summary of Peak: Secrets from the New Science of Expertise we follow the cases Ericsson built his science on: Steve Faloon's digit-memory record at Carnegie Mellon, the Tokyo study where 24 ordinary toddlers learned perfect pitch, Paul Brady training his ear at 32, London cabbies whose hippocampus grew while learning The Knowledge, Alexander Alekhine's 26 blindfold chess games, Herbert Simon's chessboards, and the Berlin violin study behind the 10,000-hour rule. Then we put the theory to work: naive vs. purposeful vs. deliberate practice, mental representations, feedback loops, Benjamin Franklin's red-ink writing method, and how to practice at work when nobody hands you a coach. We also take the strongest critique seriously: genes, luck and messy fields.
